The Old Gods are colossal, parasitic horrors of flesh and madness that plummeted from the cosmos during Azeroth's primordial dawn. Though vanquished and bound deep beneath the crust by the Titans, their ancient whispers still corrode mortal minds, twist nature, and drive doomsday cults to unearth their prisons.

Long before mortal records began, Azeroth was dominated by the Black Empire—a terrifying civilization ruled by the Old Gods: Y'Shaarj, C'Thun, Yogg-Saron, and N'Zoth. These colossal mountains of chaotic flesh embedded themselves into the planet's crust, commanding elemental armies and insectoid swarms. When the Titans arrived, their armies fought an apocalyptic war to uproot them. However, when the Titan Aman'Thul ripped Y'Shaarj from the surface, it tore a catastrophic wound into the world's crust, causing the planet's arcane lifeblood to hemorrhage. Realizing that slaying the entities outright would destroy Azeroth itself, the Titans chose to bind the surviving Old Gods in vast, subterranean prisons to keep them dormant forever.

Even chained beneath miles of stone and enchanted wards, the Old Gods have never truly slept. Their psychic malice seeps continually into the world, corrupting the vulnerable. It was their collective malice that slowly drove Neltharion the Earth-Warder mad during the War of the Ancients, twisting the noble dragon into Deathwing. When Queen Azshara and her Highborne drowned beneath the raging waters of the Great Sundering, an Old God answered their desperation, transforming them into the serpentine naga. Furthermore, their insidious taint has breached the Emerald Dream, twisting druidic realms into the creeping terror known as the Emerald Nightmare.

In the modern era, mortal civilizations treat the Old Gods as myth, yet their prisons are fracturing. Nearly a millennium ago, the insectoid qiraji swarmed out of the southern desert of Silithus in the War of the Shifting Sands, serving their master C'Thun until the night elves and dragons sealed them behind the Scarab Wall. Today, ominous cults like the Twilight's Hammer gather in dark corners across Kalimdor and the Eastern Kingdoms, performing foul rites to shatter the Titans' bindings and hasten the end of all mortal life.

The Old Horde was the blood-crazed coalition of orcish clans manipulated by demonic power into conquering Draenor and invading Azeroth. Led first by Blackhand and later by Orgrim Doomhammer, its path of destruction shaped the First and Second Wars until its decisive defeat by the Alliance of Lordaeron. Today, Thrall's New Horde seeks to overcome that dark legacy, while isolated remnants like the Dark Horde still cling to its bloody past.

Before it crossed into Azeroth, the Horde was forged on Draenor through demonic manipulation. The demon lord Kil'jaeden used the warlock Gul'dan and the elder shaman Ner'zhul to deceive the proud, spiritual orc clans into believing the draenei plotted their extermination. As elemental spirits abandoned the warring orcs, shamanistic traditions were cast aside for warlock magic. Sealed by the consumption of the blood of Mannoroth, the clans surrendered to bloodlust, slaughtering the draenei and draining their homeland of life.

With Draenor's lands withering away and resources exhausted, the warlock Gul'dan and the possessed human guardian Medivh opened the Dark Portal into Azeroth. The Horde poured through, igniting the First War against the Kingdom of Stormwind. Under Warchief Blackhand—and the covert strings of Gul'dan's Shadow Council—the Horde battered the southern realm. Toward the war's conclusion, Orgrim Doomhammer slew Blackhand and purged the Shadow Council, taking command of the Horde and razing Stormwind to the ground.

Orgrim Doomhammer drove the Horde north across the seas into the Second War, forging alliances with forest trolls and goblin mercenaries. However, at the height of the siege of Lordaeron, Gul'dan deserted the war effort with his loyalists to seek the Tomb of Sargeras. Fractured and reeling from the betrayal, the Horde was pushed back to Blackrock Mountain and crushed by the Alliance of Lordaeron. Defeated, their portal destroyed, surviving orcs were herded into internment camps, afflicted with lethargy as the demonic blood haze faded.

Originally a shamanistic clan people hailing from the alien world of Draenor, the orcs were deceived and corrupted into a bloodthirsty conquering force by the demonic Burning Legion. After invading Azeroth and suffering eventual defeat and internment, they were rallied by Warchief Thrall to reclaim their spiritual heritage. In this new era, the orcs lead the Horde from their newly carved nation of Durotar, striving for honor while grappling with the lingering shadow of their demonic past.

Before their fall, orcs lived as nomadic hunter-gatherers and spiritual clans across the rugged landscapes of Draenor. Their culture was grounded in ancestral reverence and deep communion with elemental spirits, guided primarily by revered shamans. The disparate clans—such as the Frostwolves, Warsongs, and Shadowmoon—maintained a fragile peace mediated at biannual gatherings known as the Kosh'harg festival. Though physically formidable and deeply proud, traditional orcish society was defined by survival, honor, and harmony with the natural elements rather than mindless conquest.

The fate of the orcs shattered when Kil'jaeden and the warlock Gul'dan orchestrated their corruption. Tricked into drinking the blood of the demon Mannoroth, the orcs were seized by a supernatural bloodlust that warped their natural brown skin to a sickly green. Forged into the original Horde, they nearly eradicated Draenor's draenei before pouring through the Dark Portal into Azeroth. The First and Second Wars saw human kingdoms fall and orcish armies reach Lordaeron's gates, but internal treachery and the unified Alliance of Lordaeron eventually crushed the invaders, herding survivors into miserable internment camps.

Imprisonment stripped the orcs of their demonic frenzy, leaving them lethargic and broken until Thrall, an orc raised in human captivity, escaped. Reconnecting with shamanism, Thrall rallied the Frostwolf clan, freed his kin from the camps, and established a renewed Horde. Heeding prophetic warnings, he led his people across the Great Sea to Kalimdor. There, the sacrifice of Grom Hellscream finally broke Mannoroth's blood curse forever. Today, the orcs have carved out the arid realm of Durotar and built the fortress-city of Orgrimmar, striving to maintain their hard-won honor amidst renewed tensions with the Alliance.

Paladins are holy knights of the Alliance who blend martial prowess with divine magic. Clad in heavy plate armor, they wield weapons empowered by the Holy Light to protect the innocent, heal the wounded, and strike down wicked foes.

The paladins were originally established during the Second War by Archbishop Alonsus Faol. Having witnessed the devastation wrought upon the pious Clerics of Northshire during the First War, Faol recognized that healers alone could not survive the brutality of orcish warfare. He gathered virtuous knights of Lordaeron and trained surviving clerics in the ways of martial combat and divine magic. Baptized as the Knights of the Silver Hand and led by Uther the Lightbringer, these champions provided both physical defense and spiritual renewal to the kingdoms of humanity.

Where priests act as the voice of the Holy Light—preaching faith and tending the spirits of the common folk—paladins serve as its martial arm. Their profound conviction grants them miraculous powers: they project emboldening auras, seal sanctified blessings upon their allies, and mend fatal injuries. In combat against unholy horrors, the Light burns through their strikes, allowing paladins to incinerate undead and demonic entities with righteous fury.

The fall of Lordaeron during the Third War scattered the original order, yet the ideals of the Silver Hand endure. Today, the mantle has been embraced by the humans of Stormwind and the stalwart dwarves of Ironforge. Operating out of sanctuaries like the Cathedral of Light and the Hall of Mysteries, these new paladins pledge their swords and shields to uphold justice and defend the Alliance from the gathering shadows.

Pirates and buccaneers are lawless seafaring plunderers operating across the Great Sea and coastal waters of Azeroth. Preying on Alliance, Horde, and neutral merchant vessels alike, they band together under loose flags to seize wealth, capture cargo, and control coastal coves. Their violent presence drives constant naval skirmishes from the waters of Kalimdor to the shores of the Eastern Kingdoms.

Pirates—often called buccaneers, corsairs, or freebooters—are maritime raiders of nearly every race who make their living seizing ships and raiding coastal settlements. Their operations stretch far beyond simple robbery; crews regularly engage in smuggling, kidnappings, and mercenary contracts for whoever has coin. With the chaos left behind by the Third War and the collapse of northern kingdoms, naval enforcement has fractured, giving pirate factions the freedom to carve out fortified footholds on neglected islands and coastal coves.

Despite common tales painting pirate life as one of romantic adventure, life aboard a buccaneer vessel is brutal and short. Crews endure squalid, rat-infested holds, harsh discipline, and the ever-present threat of scurvy, fought off only with supplies of limes. Betrayal is an everyday hazard, and captains maintain their command solely through strength and fear of punishment, which ranges from immediate execution to being marooned or fed to sharks. When battles end, buccaneers celebrate with roaring bouts of dice, song, and heavy rum.

While independent crews roam every sea lane, major organizations wield enough ships to contest sovereign navies. The Southsea Freebooters harass shipping throughout the waters surrounding Kalimdor, while the notorious Bloodsail Buccaneers menace the southern seas and wage open war against the Steamwheedle Cartel in Booty Bay.

The Plague of Undeath is a supernatural contagion concocted by the Lich King under the direction of the Burning Legion to scourge northern Eastern Kingdoms. Transmitted through infected grain, airborne cauldrons, and tainted waterways, the sickness rapidly kills living mortals and raises them as mind-bound thralls of the Scourge.

The plague was devised by the fallen shaman Ner'zhul after he was transformed into the Lich King by Kil'jaeden. From his icy seat atop the Frozen Throne in Northrend, Ner'zhul perfected the sickness as an unholy vanguard for the Burning Legion's invasion. Testing his power on isolated human villages across Northrend, he discovered that he could snuff out life and psychically command the corpses that arose shortly after. Ner'zhul's telepathic summon reached across the Great Sea to the Kirin Tor mage Kel'Thuzad, who abandoned Dalaran to serve the entity. Kel'Thuzad organized the secretive Cult of the Damned, whose mortal infiltrators laid the groundwork to poison Lordaeron from within.

Kel'Thuzad and the dreadlord Mal'Ganis chose Lordaeron's agricultural heartland to distribute the contagion. The cult secured distribution centers around Andorhal, packaging the plague into crates of grain destined for population centers across the north, including Brill and Stratholme. Unsuspecting villagers baked bread with the contaminated shipments, falling sick with burning joints, oozing sores, and milky eyes. Within three days, entire communities perished, only to immediately rise as flesh-eating zombies bound to the Lich King's psychic call. Prince Arthas Menethil raced to intercept the shipments, culminating in the horrific culling of Stratholme's citizens before the infected bread could transform them into Mal'Ganis's army.

The blight extends far beyond humanity. While non-human fauna generally suffer sickening fevers or rot rather than rising as undead thralls, the land itself bears the brunt of demonic and necromantic decay. Across the Plaguelands, massive plague cauldrons pump alchemical and magical vapors directly into the atmosphere, corrupting the surrounding land, where carrion grubs and colossal spore-choked mushrooms thrive. The Argent Dawn actively battles this airborne corruption by sabotaging these cauldrons, reversing their catalytic mixtures to burn the Scourge rather than feed it. Meanwhile, in the Undercity, the Royal Apothecary Society experiments tirelessly to refine a New Plague designed to slay both living foes and the undead.

Priests are spiritual guides and conduits of immense unseen power who shape belief, mend flesh, and guard souls. Channeling the radiant energies of faith or plumbing the terrifying depths of the Void, they serve as the vital heart of any war party. Across Azeroth, their traditions range from the Church of the Holy Light to the Moon Goddess's Sisterhood and shadowy Forsaken cults.

Priests guide the spiritual destiny of their communities. While physical combatants test their mettle with steel, priests draw power directly from conviction. Through divine connection, they soothe grievous wounds, raise fallen companions from death's threshold, and weave mystic barriers to repel incoming harm. Their presence on the field often marks the difference between survival and annihilation.

The priesthood is not solely an instrument of benevolence. Just as life holds both illumination and darkness, the priest walks a perilous line between divine restoration and mental devastation. Those who master the holy arts call down searing righteous vengeance to smite enemies, while practitioners of Shadow magic delve into the Void to dominate minds, twist willpower, and inflict agonizing pain from afar.

No single faith defines Azeroth's priests. In human and dwarven lands, the Church of the Holy Light codifies a philosophy of virtue, having adapted its fragile Clerics of Northshire into a hardened order after the First War. In Kalimdor, the night elven Sisterhood of Elune honors the Mother Moon with starlight and grace, while troll witch doctors beseech the primal Loa. Among the newly risen Forsaken, many have turned from former dogmas toward the Cult of the Forgotten Shadow, preaching that darkness and light must exist in delicate equilibrium.

Quilboar are aggressive, boar-like humanoids native to central Kalimdor, renowned for their sharp spinal quills and relentless territorial savagery. Claiming descent from the fallen demigod Agamaggan, they dwell within dense mazes of razor-sharp brambles across Durotar, Mulgore, and the Barrens. Their fierce struggle over water, soil, and sacred ground makes them a constant threat to travelers and Horde settlements.

Quilboar revere Agamaggan, the colossal boar Ancient who perished battling the Burning Legion during the War of the Ancients ten thousand years ago. According to their sacred traditions, the quilboar are his mortal offspring. Where Agamaggan bled and died across central Kalimdor, enormous thorny vines erupted from the scorched earth, forming sprawling root-mazes that the quilboar treat as holy ground. His crystallized blood endures across the Barrens as crimson Blood Shards, which their geomancers dig up and revere as powerful talismans.

Rather than building traditional towns of stone or timber, quilboar cultivate colossal briars that choke surrounding vegetation and render nearby ground barren. Tribes are typically guided by powerful geomancers—practitioners of an earthbound, crude shamanism who consult stones and crystals to direct the clan. These mystics call upon Agamaggan's spirit to summon spectral boars into combat. Because the arid central plains offer few oases, quilboar view water as the ultimate treasure; they stage lavish feasts when rare rains fall and defend water holes with vicious tenacity.

For generations, quilboar clashed bitterly with the nomadic tauren and roaming centaur packs. When Thrall led the Orcish Horde into Kalimdor, orcs rapidly colonized Durotar and established trade routes through the Barrens, driving displaced tribes into open revolt. Quilboar war parties ambush supply wagons, are suspected of frightening tallstriders into wagon trains, and stage raids on outposts like Crossroads and Camp Taurajo. Two principal tribes dominate the open plains: the Razormane and the Bristleback, both engaged in simultaneous feuds against the Horde and each other.

The spiritual heart of quilboar civilization lies at the southern edge of the Barrens within Razorfen Kraul and the adjacent Razorfen Downs, tangled mazes formed directly from Agamaggan's gargantuan remains. An ambitious crone named Charlga Razorflank seized dominion over the Kraul, orchestrating aggressive assaults against rival clans and Horde territories. Worse still, the traditional quilboar capital of Razorfen Downs has fallen under the sway of the Scourge. In league with the lich Amnennar the Coldbringer, corrupted Death's Head quilboar have succumbed to undeath, turning the ancestral tomb into a plague-ridden redoubt.

Now, the tribes view every caravan, outpost, and water well as stolen ancestral ground.

They test and recruit only the most cunning operatives across Azeroth, valuing peerless discipline, stealth, and lethal efficiency above all else.

Tucked away in the craggy mountains connecting Hillsbrad to Alterac, Ravenholdt Manor serves as the nerve center for Azeroth's premier brotherhood of assassins. Led by Lord Jorach Ravenholdt, the organization operates far beyond the jurisdiction of kings and warchiefs. Within its walls, master specialists hone every lethal art: Master Kang instructs disciples in close combat and assassination, the Thunderwood brothers brew rare and deadly poisons, and gnome craftsmen engineer intricate locks to test fledglings. To non-rogues, entering the estate is an overt flirtation with death, where an unwary step easily ends with a poisoned dagger in the ribs.

For years, Ravenholdt has been locked in an escalating feud with the Syndicate, an aristocratic criminal cartel infesting Alterac and Arathi. While the League regards the Syndicate as clumsy, arrogant amateurs, their sheer numbers make them impossible to eradicate through simple slaughter. Instead, Ravenholdt employs psychological and structural disruption: by tasking contracted rogues with pickpocketing the signet emblems worn by Syndicate ringleaders, the League relies on the Syndicate's own paranoia and cutthroat hierarchy to execute disgraced members internally.

Though Ravenholdt cooperates on occasion with other intelligence apparatuses like Stormwind's SI:7, they answer to no crown. Throughout the violent history of Azeroth, constant warfare has repeatedly driven civilian populations from their homes. From the exodus of Stormwind during the First War to the tragic flight from Lordaeron in the Third War, refugees remain living testaments to the devastating costs of invasion, plague, and betrayal.

When the Orcish Horde swept through the kingdom of Stormwind during the First War, settlements like Goldshire, Moonbrook, and Grand Hamlet burned. Following the assassination of King Llane Wrynn, Sir Anduin Lothar took command of the kingdom's remnants. He gathered surviving soldiers and desperate civilians, escorting them to the harbor as the city burned. While some citizens hid in the catacombs beneath the Cathedral of Light, Lothar led a massive fleet across the Great Sea to the northern shores of Lordaeron. Arriving at Southshore, the exiled survivors—including the young Prince Varian Wrynn and High Clerist Lady Mara Fordragon—were granted sanctuary by King Terenas Menethil II.

A generation after welcoming Stormwind's exiles, the people of Lordaeron faced ruin of their own. During the Third War, the Scourge plague and the legions of the undead systematically dismantled the kingdom. Prince Arthas Menethil slaughtered his own subjects as he swept across the realm, leaving survivors scattered and terrified. Lady Jaina Proudmoore managed to lead an expedition of refugees across the sea to Kalimdor, eventually establishing a settlement at Theramore. However, countless others remained behind in the Eastern Kingdoms, hunted relentlessly by the Scourge, the Forsaken, and monstrous horrors that arose in the ruins.

For decades, the Riverpaw clan prowled the fringes of human civilization, but their boldness has surged in recent years. In Westfall, they roam across the Dust Plains and along the coasts, ambushing solitary travelers and raiding homesteads. Beyond petty ambushes, the Riverpaws exhibit an unusual drive for conquest and labor. Rogues are masters of stealth, espionage, and sudden, lethal combat who dictate the terms of engagement from the shadows. Relying on light leather armor, dual-wielded blades, and brewed toxins, they strike unawares before vanishing back into the dark. Across Azeroth, they serve as scouts, assassins, pickpockets, and agents for factions and hidden syndicates alike.

Rogues eschew the heavy plate and open confrontation of traditional frontline warriors. Clad in lightweight leather to remain completely silent and mobile, they stalk their quarry unseen. When they engage, they seize the opening moments through precision and surprise, aiming for vital organs or exposed joints. Utilizing an ever-flowing pool of energy and rapid weapon combinations, a rogue softens up an enemy with carefully chained strikes before unleashing a catastrophic finishing blow.

A blade alone is rarely enough for a professional cutpurse or killer. Rogues are skilled alchemists of lethal concoctions, hand-crafting venomous coatings to numb limbs, slow escapes, or rapidly sap the vitality of their targets. Coupled with lockpicking tools, thrown weapons, and distracting trickery, they excel at slipping past fortified perimeters, disarming traps, and infiltrating vaults that would stump a company of soldiers.

While many rogues operate as lone wolves, highwaymen, or street-level thugs, the finest operatives belong to organized intelligence networks and assassin guilds. Stormwind relies on the clandestine operatives of SI:7, Ironforge harbors the covert Hidden Circle, and the Forsaken utilize the relentless Deathstalkers. In Orgrimmar, the shadowy remnants of the Shattered Hand serve the Warchief, while the elite, neutral League of Assassins answers to Lord Jorach Ravenholdt.

Their preeminent endeavor is the creation of a 'New Plague'—a concoction intended to eradicate the Scourge and destroy the Lich King. Gilneas is a secluded human kingdom occupying a rugged, storm-lashed peninsula south of Silverpine Forest. Following the Second War, King Genn Greymane severed ties with the outside world and locked his nation behind the colossal Greymane Wall, leaving neighboring territories abandoned and the kingdom shrouded in total isolation.

Gilneas was once an assertive maritime powerhouse among the human realms, claiming lineage from the ancient empire of Arathor. King Genn Greymane participated reluctantly in the Second War, believing his kingdom could defend itself without foreign entanglements. Bitter over the loss of Gilnean lives and unwilling to help finance the internment camps for captured orcs, Greymane severed relations with the Alliance of Lordaeron. To permanently shield his realm from outside calamity, he ordered the construction of a massive stone barricade along the kingdom's northern frontier.

Erecting the Greymane Wall demanded painful geopolitical compromises. The natural mountain passes used to anchor the ramparts cleaved straight through the holdings of Lord Darius Crowley. As a consequence, territories such as Ambermill and Pyrewood Village were cut off on the northern side, stranded outside the gate. When the Scourge swept across Lordaeron during the Third War, King Greymane refused entreaties for aid and barred the doors to human refugees, leaving the surrounding villages to face the plague and the undead alone.

Darkness gathered just beyond the wall. During the Third War, the Dalaran archmage Arugal summoned feral worgen to bolster the Kirin Tor against the Scourge. The beasts slaughtered the undead, then turned on the wizards themselves, besieged Baron Silverlaine's keep and spread through the shadows of Silverpine. Today, Gilneas remains locked behind sealed gates and treacherous sea reefs, an impenetrable enigma steeped in eerie rumors and total silence.

Before his fall, Sargeras was the greatest and noblest warrior among the titans. Entrusted by the Pantheon of Order to safeguard their grand creations across the Great Dark Beyond, he waged war against the chaotic demons spawned from the Twisting Nether. Incapable of conceiving pure evil, Sargeras trapped countless fiends away within the prison world of Mardum. Yet eons of relentless warfare against cosmic horrors gradually wore down his altruistic spirit.

While traversing the cosmos, Sargeras encountered a world thoroughly corrupted by the monstrous Old Gods and learned of the dark powers lurking in the Void. Horrified by the prospect of a slumbering titan worldsoul falling into utter corruption, he concluded that creation was fundamentally flawed. Believing that a lifeless universe was preferable to one consumed by void, he shattered Mardum, bathed himself in chaotic fel fire, and marshaled the liberated demons into the unstoppable Burning Legion.

Satyrs are twisted, caprine demons born from the curse of the Highborne sorcerer Xavius during the ancient War of the Ancients. Once night elves, they were warped by Sargeras into horned, hooved beasts dedicated to spreading fel corruption, tormenting their former kin, and furthering the Burning Legion's will. Across the wilds of Kalimdor, scattered satyr sects corrupt pristine woodlands, desecrate moonwells, and subvert vulnerable mortal cults.

Ten thousand years ago during the War of the Ancients, the Highborne councilor Xavius failed to keep the Burning Legion's initial gateway stable against Malfurion Stormrage. Enraged by this blunder, Sargeras dismantled Xavius's spirit and rebuilt him as a punishment and tool: his torso retained elven features, but he gained wicked horns, taloned claws, a leonine tail, and the cloven lower body of a goat. Sent back into Zin-Azshari, Xavius gleefully passed his fel affliction to other power-hungry Highborne. Though Xavius was struck down, his demonic progeny survived, continually seeking to reproduce their kind by corrupting others.

Following the Great Sundering, the surviving demons and satyrs regrouped to wage the War of the Satyr against the shattered night elf civilization. Desperate to counter the satyrs' vicious demonic magic, night elven druids unleashed the unruly Pack Form, inadvertently giving birth to the first feral worgen. The worgen tore through the satyr hosts, shattering their unified army. Robbed of central leadership, the remnants fractured into scattered sects, lingering in dark forests and ancient ruins while harboring deep hatred for their kaldorei cousins.

Today, satyr clans inhabit deep woodland enclaves across Kalimdor, from Darkshore and Ashenvale to Felwood, Azshara, and Feralas. They feed directly on the land's pure magic, leeching and spoiling nature until their hooves swell with drained arcane energy. Satyrs frequently turn peaceful furbolg tribes violent, taint ancient moonwells, and serve as covert liaisons for the Shadow Council and the Burning Blade. While some work alongside Twilight's Hammer cultists or hide within ancient ruins like Dire Maul, all remain bound to the shadow of the Burning Legion.

The Second War was the continent-spanning clash across the Eastern Kingdoms between the Orcish Horde and the newly forged Alliance of Lordaeron. In the final mountain passes of the Burning Steppes, Anduin Lothar fell in single combat against Doomhammer, but his lieutenant Turalyon rallied the troops and routed the orcs. Shaman are the spiritual mediators and elemental guides of the Horde, communing with the primordial forces of earth, air, fire, and water. Balancing raw nature through totems, lightning, and ancestral healing, they serve as the spiritual core of orc, tauren, and troll culture under the leadership of Warchief Thrall.

Unlike priests who revere the divine or mages who bend the arcane, shaman interact directly with the primal forces of nature. The elements of earth, air, fire, and water are inherently chaotic and locked in perpetual conflict. A shaman does not enslave these forces, but petitions and negotiates with them, serving as a balance keeper between primal fury and the mortal world. Through wooden and stone totems planted into the soil, shaman channel these elemental bargains to protect allies, hinder foes, or mend the wounded with cleansing water.

Shamanism was once the ancient foundation of orcish clan life on Draenor. However, Kil'jaeden and the Shadow Council deceived the shamans into war against the draenei, causing the elemental spirits to withdraw their favor. Stripped of their gifts, many former shaman succumbed to demonic corruption and became warlocks, nearly extinguishing the tradition entirely. Only after the Second War did Thrall, guided by Drek'Thar of the Frostwolf clan, rediscover the ancient rites. Shan'do is a revered Darnassian honorific meaning "honored teacher" or "honored instructor." Traditionally used within night elven society and druidic circles, it denotes deep reverence toward a mentor who guides another along the path of wisdom and natural magic. Its direct counterpart is thero'shan, meaning "honored student."

In the Darnassian language, shan'do translates directly to "honored teacher" or "honored instructor." The prefix "shan" carries the meaning of honor, while the suffix "do" denotes authority, seniority, or mastery—a linguistic root shared with words like minn'do ("mother"). It is far more than an occupational label: addressing an elder or mentor as shan'do expresses solemn humility, filial devotion, and enduring respect for their guidance.

Following the Sundering, the Shen'dralar of Eldre'Thalas languished without the Well of Eternity. Prince Tortheldrin devised a dark salvation: summon the demon Immol'thar and siphon its power. The Steamwheedle Cartel is the largest and most influential goblin enterprise operating across modern Azeroth. Fiercely neutral, the cartel governs bustling commercial hubs like Booty Bay, Ratchet, and Gadgetzan, serving Alliance and Horde patrons alike so long as their coin is genuine. Originating from the subterranean goblin capital of Undermine, the Steamwheedle Cartel initially allied with the Old Horde during the Second War, supplying war machines, sappers, and naval engineering. After the dust settled, the cartel's leaders realized that picking sides cost more than it earned. Embracing absolute neutrality, they expanded across both continents, opening trade networks that welcome Alliance and Horde alike. The cartel's influence rests on strategic ports and frontier towns. The Stonemasons Guild was the collective of master builders and artisans responsible for reconstructing Stormwind City and Nethergarde Keep after the Second War. Following a bitter dispute over payment with the House of Nobles that ended in deadly riots, the guild was forcibly dissolved, driving its members into exile and giving rise to the Defias Brotherhood.

Following the devastation of the First and Second Wars, the Alliance of Lordaeron commissioned the Stonemasons Guild to erect Nethergarde Keep in the Blasted Lands to monitor the shattered Dark Portal. Led by elected Guildmaster Edwin VanCleef, the artisans demonstrated a mastery of masonry that rivaled the Royal Stonecutters Union of the dwarves. Impressed by their labor, the House of Nobles hired the guild to embark upon the monumental task of rebuilding Stormwind City from ruins, trusting them to restore the capital to its ancient grandeur.

For years, VanCleef and an army of craftsmen toiled through Elwynn, raising the soaring spires of Stormwind Keep and the massive arches of the Cathedral of Light. However, royal finances collapsed under heavy military debts incurred in southern campaigns. Influenced by aristocratic politics, the House of Nobles refused to pay the guild their agreed salaries and fees. When VanCleef petitioned for restitution, the nobles answered by unilaterally disbanding the guild, sparking immense fury among the laborers who had bled to rebuild the city.

The wage dispute erupted into violent unrest throughout Stormwind. During a desperate effort to broker peace, Queen Tiffin Wrynn was struck and killed by a thrown projectile, sending King Varian into profound grief and vengeance. The Crown cracked down ruthlessly, capturing key conspirators like VanCleef's lieutenant, Bazil Thredd, while VanCleef and hundreds of ruined stonemasons fled into the countryside of Westfall. Exiled and branded as traitors, the desperate artisans transformed their trade union into the militant Defias Brotherhood.

The standoff between the nobility and the builders was not merely a matter of bankrupt coffers. Behind the scenes, the royal court advisor Lady Katrana Prestor actively fanned the embers of discord. She convinced the aristocracy that the Stonemasons' bills were extortionate and their work shoddy, while simultaneously provoking the craftsmen into outright rebellion. By paralyzing Stormwind with internal strife and cutting off supplies to Westfall, the black dragon Onyxia successfully fractured the kingdom from within.

The Stormwind Army is the standing military force charged with defending the Kingdom of Stormwind and preserving the security of the Grand Alliance in the south. Though legendary for its resilient knights and marshals, the army is currently crippled by royal absence, political infighting, and crippling troop shortages across the provinces.
A Legacy of Iron and Blood

The army traces its martial lineage through centuries of brutal conflict, from early frontier clashes against gnolls to the desperate defense against the Gurubashi trolls. In the First War, under King Llane Wrynn I and Sir Anduin Lothar, the Knights of Stormwind mounted legendary ambushes against the Orcish Horde, yet fell when the capital burned. Surviving remnants evacuated to Lordaeron, spearheading the formation of the Alliance of Lordaeron and fighting through the Second War. After the Dark Portal's fall, General Turalyon helped reform and train a renewed Stormwind military alongside a restored kingdom.

Headquartered within Stormwind Keep, the military relies on dedicated regional garrisons overseen by the Stormwind Marshals. Within the stone walls of the capital, the Stormwind City Guard maintains civil order, while the elite Royal Guard attends the boy-king Anduin Wrynn and Highlord Bolvar Fordragon. Beyond the gates, the army deploys outposts to patrol Elwynn Forest, keep order along trade roads, and man defensive ramparts as far as the Redridge Mountains, assisted on the water by the Stormwind Fleet.

Despite its proud traditions, the modern army is stretched beyond its breaking point. Debts incurred by the House of Nobles to expand military reach into Stranglethorn fueled the bitter rift with the Stonemasons Guild, culminating in civil riots, Queen Tiffin's death, and the birth of the Defias Brotherhood. With King Varian missing, the House of Nobles has routinely withheld troops, funding, and supplies from outlying settlements like Westfall, Lakeshire, and Duskwood, forcing local marshals to deputize wandering adventurers to carry the realm's burdens.

The Kingdom of Stormwind is the southernmost and currently foremost human realm on Azeroth, holding dominion over Elwynn Forest, Westfall, Duskwood, and the Redridge Mountains. Sacked and shattered during the First War, it was rebuilt through blood and labor after the Second, rising to become the military and cultural center of the Alliance following the tragic collapse of Lordaeron in the north. Today, the kingdom stands beset from within and without, ruled by the ten-year-old King Anduin Wrynn under the watchful guidance of Highlord Bolvar Fordragon while its crowned monarch remains missing.

Stormwind was established over a thousand years ago by descendants of the ancient Arathi empire who ventured south beyond the crags of Khaz Modan into fertile, forested valleys. For centuries, the northern kingdoms dismissed Stormwind as an isolated, rural hinterland, even ignoring desperate pleas for aid during the Gnoll War. Led by King Barathen Wrynn, the realm defeated the gnolls and later the Gurubashi trolls alone, forging a culture fiercely proud of its self-reliance and the Light.

That independence was nearly extinguished when the Orcish Horde poured through the Dark Portal. Stormwind City burned to ash in the First War, its King Llane slain. The surviving populace fled north across the Great Sea led by Sir Anduin Lothar, rallying the northern realms into the Alliance of Lordaeron. Once the Orcish threat was crushed in the Second War, refugees returned home, hiring the Stonemasons Guild to rebuild their magnificent capital of white stone and blue banners. When the Scourge wiped out Lordaeron during the Third War, Stormwind became humanity's greatest remaining bastion.

Beneath its soaring towers, Stormwind struggles to govern its vast southern holdings. While Elwynn Forest remains relatively secure, neighboring regions like Westfall are swarming with outlaws, Redridge faces constant orc and gnoll incursions, and the darkened woods of Duskwood have fallen out of the realm's control. A bitter dispute between the House of Nobles and the Stonemasons sparked the violent Defias riot that took the life of Queen Tiffin, scattering displaced workers into open rebellion across the provinces.

The kingdom's instability deepened with the sudden, quiet disappearance of King Varian Wrynn while sailing to a diplomatic summit with the Horde at Theramore. To preserve fragile public order, the crown was placed on his ten-year-old son, Anduin Wrynn, with Highlord Bolvar Fordragon named Lord Regent. Yet royal authority is divided and stalled: the House of Nobles, guided closely by the enigmatic Lady Katrana Prestor, repeatedly vetoes military deployments, leaving local towns to fend for themselves while dangerous secrets fester within Stormwind Keep.

The Syndicate is a widespread human criminal organization founded and led by dispossessed nobles of the fallen kingdom of Alterac. Operating out of fortified strongholds across the Alterac Mountains, Hillsbrad Foothills, and the ruins of Stromgarde Keep, they wage an uncompromising war against both the Alliance and the Horde to restore their lost aristocracy.

When the kingdom of Alterac collapsed in dishonor following King Aiden Perenolde's treachery during the Second War, its aristocracy was stripped of land and title. Refusing to accept their exile, the remaining Alteraci nobility banded together under the late king's son, Prince Aliden Perenolde. Adopting distinctive orange bandanas and standardizing their ranks with hired thugs, highwaymen, and hedge wizards, they forged the Syndicate. To the outside world, they behave like common brigands, raiding caravans, ambushing travelers, and running extortion rings. In truth, their criminal enterprises exist solely to fund an organized effort to reconquer their ancestral domains and subjugate surrounding lands.

The Syndicate maintains entrenched footholds across northern Lordaeron. In the snowy Alterac Mountains, they fortified the ruined town of Strahnbrad and established encampments throughout the Uplands and Dandred's Fold. To the south, they hold the crumbling remnants of Durnholde Keep in the Hillsbrad Foothills, using it as a springboard to harass Southshore and raid supply routes. Further east across the Thoradin's Wall, Lord Falconcrest marshals an occupying Syndicate army inside the historic ruins of Stromgarde Keep in Arathi, actively battling the battered Stromgarde Militia for mastery over the Arathi Highlands.

Unlike ordinary outlaws, the Syndicate harbors grand ideological ambitions that earn them the hatred of almost every regional faction. They view the Alliance as mortal enemies who stole their rightful heritage, frequently targeting Southshore officials such as Magistrate Henry Maleb. Towards the Horde, their stance is openly supremacist: following the philosophies of Aedelas Blackmoore, they view orcs merely as beasts fit for slave labor and seek to rebuild the internment camp system. Sylvanas Windrunner's Forsaken execute captured Syndicate members on sight, while the clandestine thieves' guild of Ravenholdt wages a constant shadow war against their sloppy, arrogant operatives.

While the Syndicate's noble leaders believe they are fighting for human supremacy and their birthright, they are being steered from within by darker masters. Cultists belonging to the Argus Wake have thoroughly infiltrated their upper ranks, manipulating men like Lord Falconcrest into seizing Stromgarde Keep. Far from serving human interests, the Argus Wake ultimately reports to the Shadow Council based in Felwood's Jaedenar, using the Syndicate's armies and stolen territories as a mortal vanguard to clear the way for the Burning Legion.

The tauren, or shu'halo in their native tongue, are a noble race of nomadic bovine humanoids native to central Kalimdor. Deeply devoted to the Earth Mother, shamanism, and the natural world, they were driven near extinction by ruthless centaur clans before forging a bond with Thrall's New Horde. Today, united under High Chieftain Cairne Bloodhoof, they have established a permanent home across the verdant plains of Mulgore and the high rises of Thunder Bluff.

For countless generations, the tauren lived as seasonal nomads wandering the arid plains of the Barrens, hunting the great kodo and listening for the voice of the Earth Mother. However, their peaceful wanderings were plagued by centuries of brutal bloodshed. The ferocious centaur tribes, born from the tragic union of Zaetar and Princess Theradras, waged an unrelenting war of extermination against them. Lacking a fortified homeland and reluctant to wage endless war, the tauren tribes were pushed to the brink of annihilation, their very survival hanging by a thread.
The New Horde and Thunder Bluff

Survival came from an unexpected alliance across the sea. During the Third War, Chieftain Cairne Bloodhoof encountered Warchief Thrall and his newly arrived orcs. Recognizing a shared spirit of honor and a longing for shamanic heritage, the two leaders joined forces. With the Horde's assistance, the tauren crushed the marauding centaur and claimed the lush, sheltered grasslands of Mulgore. Upon its windswept mesas, Cairne raised the city of Thunder Bluff. Indebted by this salvation, the tauren marched alongside the Horde to Mount Hyjal to turn back the Burning Legion.

Within the Horde, the tauren act as a steadying, peaceful conscience. Their mastery of nature and the elements helped revitalize orcish shamanism, while Archdruid Hamuul Runetotem fosters rare diplomatic and spiritual ties with night elf druids to investigate the growing corruption within the Emerald Dream. Yet unity remains fragile. While most tribes revere Cairne's wisdom, the xenophobic and ruthless Grimtotem clan, headed by the scheming elder crone Magatha, resides within Thunder Bluff while secretly plotting to usurp leadership and steer the shu'halo toward supremacy.

King Terenas Menethil II was the venerable sovereign of Lordaeron who ruled for over five decades and forged the original Alliance of Lordaeron during the Second War. Renowned as a wise and diplomatic leader, he shielded humanity from the initial Horde invasion and sheltered the young Prince Varian Wrynn. His tragic murder by his corrupted son, Prince Arthas, directly triggered the collapse of Lordaeron to the Scourge.

When refugees from Stormwind arrived in the north led by Sir Anduin Lothar, King Terenas Menethil II answered their call. Convening the monarchs of the fractured human kingdoms alongside envoys from Ironforge and Quel'Thalas, Terenas orchestrated the formation of the Alliance of Lordaeron. Rather than seizing military command for himself, he wisely nominated Lothar as supreme commander, uniting humanity's kingdoms for the first time in millennia to triumph over the Old Horde.

In the wake of the Second War, Terenas insisted upon placing surviving orcs into internment camps rather than executing them, believing that peace could be preserved if their demonic fury dissipated. This humane but costly decision placed staggering taxes on Lordaeron's allies. Gilneas sealed itself behind the Greymane Wall, Stromgarde seceded over political disputes, and the high elves withdrew entirely, leaving Terenas to shoulder the burden with a fracturing coalition.

In his twilight years, Terenas faced rising orc revolts led by Thrall, whispers of northern death cults, and a mysterious plague. When a wandering prophet warned the king to abandon Lordaeron and flee across the sea to Kalimdor, Terenas dismissed him as a madman. Shortly after, Prince Arthas returned from his northern campaign hailed as a victor. In the midst of the royal celebrations, Arthas knelt before his father, drew the runeblade Frostmourne, and ran Terenas through the heart, shattering the kingdom forever.

The Third War was the apocalyptic conflict that shattered the old world order just a few years ago. Orchestrated by the Burning Legion and unleashed through the Lich King's Plague of Undeath, the war saw the fall of the Kingdom of Lordaeron and the near-total destruction of Quel'Thalas before culminating in a desperate, unified stand at Mount Hyjal.

The war began subtly in northern Lordaeron, disguised as a virulent sickness carried in infected grain distributed from Andorhal. The tainted harvest did not merely slaughter its victims; it raised them as ravenous ghouls bound to the Lich King's will. Prince Arthas Menethil raced to stem the contagion alongside the Kirin Tor sorceress Jaina Proudmoore. Blinded by grief, fury, and dreadlord manipulations, Arthas purged the infected population of Stratholme before pursuing his foe to the frozen waste of Northrend. There, he took up the cursed runeblade Frostmourne, casting aside his soul. He returned south only to murder his father, King Terenas, delivering Lordaeron into the hands of the Scourge.

Empowered by death, Arthas crushed the high elven realm of Quel'Thalas to resurrect the necromancer Kel'Thuzad at the Sunwell. The undead army then laid siege to Dalaran, seizing the spellbooks necessary to summon the demon lord Archimonde into Azeroth. With the commander of the Burning Legion walking mortal soil, Dalaran was leveled in an arcane display of devastation. The Scourge had served its purpose as an advance guard, and the Burning Legion turned its sights toward the eternal power resting across the Great Sea.
The Flight West and Mount Hyjal

Guided by cryptic warnings from the mysterious Prophet—later revealed as the redeemed Guardian Medivh—Warchief Thrall led the New Horde across the Great Sea, while Lady Jaina Proudmoore evacuated surviving Alliance refugees. In ancient Kalimdor, the newcomers clashed with the reclusive night elves before all three factions recognized the supreme threat looming over them. Beneath the World Tree Nordrassil atop Mount Hyjal, mortals stood together against impossible odds. Archimonde was destroyed by ancestral wisps when he reached the tree, shattering the Legion's vanguard and ending the war.

Although Archimonde fell, the peace of 25 ADP is fragile and stained with loss. The Alliance of Lordaeron is gone, leaving the kingdom of Stormwind and Ironforge to anchor the southern Alliance while Lordaeron sits rotting as the Plaguelands. In Kalimdor, Thrall's Horde carved out Durotar, yet tensions with the newly allied night elves remain volatile. The Scourge endures in the northern ruins, and the freed undead—the Forsaken—now hold the catacombs of Capital City, waging a war of survival against both former masters and vengeful crusaders.

The titans are a primordial race of colossal, godlike beings who wander the cosmos bringing order and shaping worlds. In ancient antiquity, they came to Azeroth to vanquish the chaotic Old Gods, establish massive terrestrial facilities, and foster life before departing into the Great Dark Beyond.

The titans are cosmic giants forged from primordial matter and arcane magic, embodying the forces of order and creation. In their journeys across the Great Dark Beyond, they sought out slumbering worlds to cultivate, raising up continents, calming chaotic elemental forces, and designing life. To enforce balance, they established powerful constructs made of stone, iron, and sea to watch over their works.

Long ago, the Pantheon of titans discovered Azeroth in the grip of the chaotic elemental lords and the horrific Old Gods. The titans waged war against these parasitic horrors, banishing the elementals to pocket planes and sealing the monstrous Old Gods deep beneath the crust of the earth. Upon securing the world, they carved great biomes, established vault complexes like Uldaman, and entrusted five great dragons—the Dragon Aspects—with stewardship of the land, magic, time, and life itself before journeying back among the stars.

Not all titans remained aligned with the Pantheon's vision of perfect order. Sargeras, once the greatest warrior and defender of the titans, grew despondent and terrified by the deep cosmic darkness and demonic malevolence he was charged with combating. Rejecting the work of his kin, Sargeras turned to nihilism, founding the demonic Burning Legion to extinguish all creation rather than allow it to be corrupted.

Trolls are among the oldest sentient races native to Azeroth, having arisen around the Well of Eternity long before the Sundering. Renowned for their incredible physical regeneration, worship of primal spirits known as loa, and mastery of voodoo, their fractured empires once ruled vast swaths of the ancient world. Today, while ancient kingdoms like the Gurubashi and Amani remain deeply hostile to outsiders, the Darkspear tribe has found a lasting haven within Thrall's Horde.

Long before the Great Sundering shattered ancient Kalimdor, the primal energies of the Well of Eternity nurtured the rise of trollkind. Emerging as savage, highly agile hunter-gatherers, the early trolls possessed a unique physiology that granted them astonishing regenerative powers, allowing them to recover rapidly from grievous wounds and even regrow severed limbs over time. Settling around the sacred mountains of Zandalar, they directed their reverence toward Kalimdor's elusive Wild Gods, whom they called loa. Under the spiritual guidance of shadow hunters and witch doctors, these rituals coalesced into the practice of voodoo and the construction of holy temple peaks like Zuldazar.

Roughly sixteen thousand years ago, curious trolls unwittingly broke an ancient taboo, awakening the C'Thraxxi horror Kith'ix. The beast rallied the aqiri swarms from the underground warrens, threatening to consume all mortal life. Faced with total annihilation, the disparate tribes united under the Zandalari to forge the Empire of Zul. Through relentless guerrilla ambushes and the summoned might of the loa, the trolls drove back the swarms. Driven to eradicate the insectoid threat, mighty tribes branched outward across the continent: the Drakkari seized the frozen north, the Gurubashi battered the aqir in the southwest, and the fierce Amani slew Kith'ix itself, founding their city of Zul'Aman upon the monster's bones.

With the insect swarms broken and contained, the unity of the Empire of Zul dissolved. Each great faction withdrew into its own sovereign empire, developing distinct cultures, physical traits, and tribal hierarchies adapted to forests, jungles, and frozen wastes. Over millennia of separation, rivalry, and territorial wars against younger races, troll dominion slowly decayed into ruin and insularity. Most remaining troll kingdoms view all other races with fierce, unyielding hostility, clinging bitterly to the ruins of their former greatness. Only the exile jungle trolls of the Darkspear tribe have chosen a new path, joining the Horde alongside orcs and tauren.

The Twilight's Hammer is a nihilistic, apocalyptic cult dedicated to awakening the Old Gods and bringing about the end of Azeroth. Originally an orcish clan led by the ogre-mage Cho'gall, it has evolved into a secretive, multiracial order actively conducting dark rituals across Kalimdor and the Eastern Kingdoms.

The Twilight's Hammer began on Draenor as an exiled clan of Pale orcs residing in the cavernous Underpale beneath Oshu'gun. Communion with Void forces drove them to embrace a grim prophecy: the Hour of Twilight, an inevitable cosmic doom when shadow engulfs all existence. Seeking to bend their terrifying shadow magic to the Horde's war effort, Gul'dan sent the two-headed ogre-mage Cho'gall to lead them. Cho'gall convinced the Pale that the Horde was merely an engine of destruction meant to usher in their beloved apocalypse. Bound by this prophecy, the clan codified their mad teachings into the Twilight Canticle—pages crafted from the flayed, inscribed skin of the Pale themselves.

When the Twilight's Hammer crossed the Dark Portal during the First War, their apocalyptic fanaticism only deepened. In the soil of Azeroth, the cultists sensed the genuine whispers of the Old Gods—ancient horrors chained beneath the earth. Blackhand tolerated their erratic, ritualistic behavior solely because Cho'gall managed their bloodlust, deploying them alongside Kilrogg Deadeye's Bleeding Hollow clan in early assaults on Stormwind Keep. The clan later operated deep within Grim Batol during the Second War, overseeing critical refineries until Gul'dan's betrayal fractured the Horde. Though Orgrim Doomhammer ordered the traitorous clan butchered near the Tomb of Sargeras, Cho'gall and a core cadre of zealots survived and fled west across the Great Sea.

Upon reaching the forgotten shores of Kalimdor, the cult transformed from a shattered orc clan into a clandestine, multiracial conspiracy. Seducing disillusioned members of both the Alliance and the Horde, the Twilight's Hammer recruits any soul broken enough to welcome oblivion. In northern Kalimdor, led by Twilight Lord Kelris, cultists have entrenched themselves within the submerged halls of Blackfathom Deeps, feeding sacrifices to Aku'mai, a monstrous pet of the Old Gods. Further north in Darkshore, their excavators disturb the colossal fossilized remains at the Master's Glaive. Across the southern deserts of Silithus, camps of robed fanatics tend abyssal windstones, listening for the stirring of ancient horrors entombed beneath the sands.

The Venture Company is a notoriously ruthless goblin cartel focused on aggressive resource extraction, heavy industrial machinery, and logging. Unaligned with the major goblin ports like Booty Bay or Ratchet, the cartel strip-mines and clear-cuts territories across Kalimdor and the Eastern Kingdoms without regard for local populations or the natural world.

Led overall by Mogul Razdunk from afar, the Venture Company operates by a simple corporate philosophy: if it can be chopped down, drilled into, or blasted out of a mountain, they will exploit it. The cartel deploys some of the most advanced heavy machinery on Azeroth, including massive lumber-harvesting shredders, drilling rigs, and industrial refineries. Unlike traditional merchant houses that focus on shipping or retail, the Venture Company specializes in seizing raw resources by force, ignoring treaties, borders, and local sovereign rights.

The cartel's rapid expansion into Kalimdor has earned them widespread enmity. In Mulgore, Supervisor Fizsprocket pushed drilling and mining rigs into the eastern bluffs despite being formally denied mineral rights by the tauren, polluting pristine water wells across the plains. Farther north, the company turned the Barrens' Sludge Fen into a chemical sewer to power oil pumps, while claiming the Horde's former Boulder Lode Mine and running foul experiments with samophlanges and toxic brews. In Stonetalon's Windshear Crag, logging operations under the mad leper gnome Gerenzo Wrenchwhistle have decimated whole groves with colossal Super Reaper 6000 machines.

The Venture Company is widely despised even by fellow goblins. Baron Revilgaz of Booty Bay frequently contracts out strikes against their base camp and oil rig at Lake Nazferiti, seeking both to thwart their territorial encroachment and steal their cutting-edge shredder fuel regulators. The Tinkers' Union in Ratchet openly runs corporate espionage against them to pilfer engineering blueprints. Worse still, SI:7 and the Shattered Hand have discovered the company trafficking dangerous alchemical compounds: selling Zanzil's deadly mind-altering poisons to Defias necromancers in Westfall and utilizing toxic fumes to breed mutated drone laborers.

The president of the cartel is Mogul Razdunk, who governs the organization's overarching corporate ventures from afar. Day-to-day work sites across Azeroth are overseen by regional supervisors, foremen, and hired overseers such as Supervisor Fizsprocket in Mulgore, Supervisor Lugwizzle at the Sludge Fen, and Gerenzo Wrenchwhistle in Stonetalon.

Ten thousand years ago, the reckless sorcery of Queen Azshara and her Highborne tore a portal through the Well of Eternity, unleashing the demonic Burning Legion onto Azeroth. Led by the young druid Malfurion Stormrage, Priestess Tyrande Whisperwind, and commander Jarod Shadowsong, a desperate coalition of mortals and ancient forest demigods repelled the invaders. The resulting destruction of the Well triggered the Great Sundering, violently shattering the ancient continent of Kalimdor and permanently altering the face of the world.

At the height of the ancient Kaldorei Empire, Queen Azshara and her elite caste of sorcerers, the Highborne, relentlessly drew upon the vast arcane depths of the Well of Eternity. Their reckless manipulation sent massive ripples into the Great Dark Beyond, attracting Sargeras, the master of the Burning Legion. Entranced by promises of ultimate power and perfection, Azshara and her advisor Xavius opened a trans-dimensional rift within the Well. Legions of felhounds, felguard, doomguard, and monstrous commanders poured into the capital city of Zin-Azshari, slaughtering all non-Highborne and beginning their crusade to purge the world of life.

Horrified by the slaughter, night elves outside the Highborne caste rallied under the seasoned general Lord Kur'talos Ravencrest. The resistance was bolstered by remarkable heroes: the first mortal druid Malfurion Stormrage, the devout priestess of Elune Tyrande Whisperwind, and Malfurion's gifted brother Illidan. When imperial forces assassinated Ravencrest and the demon armies pressed hard, command fell to the brilliant tactician Jarod Shadowsong. Realizing the elves could not survive alone, Jarod reached across old racial boundaries, recruiting the earthen, the furbolgs, and the mountain tauren into a unified frontline against the Legion's onslaught.

The war escalated to world-shattering proportions when the demigod Cenarius rallied the ancient Wild Gods and dragonflights into the fray. Determined to stop Sargeras himself from stepping foot onto Azeroth, Malfurion and the resistance made a desperate push to collapse the portal over the Well of Eternity. Their desperate gambit succeeded in casting the demonic host back into the Twisting Nether, but the strain proved too great. The Well violently imploded, triggering the Great Sundering that shattered Kalimdor into separate continents and flooded the center of the world, birthing the Great Sea and forever marking Kaldorei culture.

Warlocks are spellcasters who bargain with dark powers, commanding demons, debilitating curses, and devastating fire and shadow magics. While deeply feared and distrusted by nearly every civilized society on Azeroth, some wield these forbidden arts in defense of their factions, turning the weapons of the Burning Legion against its own agents.

Where ordinary spellcasters see corruption and ruin, warlocks see opportunity. They achieve victory through calculated cruelty, striking from a distance while cloaked in shadow and fire. By siphoning the vital essences and souls of their enemies, warlocks fuel their most catastrophic rituals, raining brimstone from the sky and breaking minds with agonizing curses. Because they wear only simple cloth and possess little physical resilience, they rely on summoned horrors to intercept danger, willingly sacrificing demonic thralls to ensure their own survival.

A warlock's authority over the Twisting Nether begins with petty bargains and grows into iron domination. Novices learn to command mischievous imps to hurl flame, but as a practitioner's dark understanding deepens, they bind far deadlier entities: voidwalkers torn from shadowy depths to absorb physical punishment, seductive succubi capable of beguiling enemy minds, and ravenous felhunters that devour magical energies. Each summon demands dangerous ritual focus, for the Nether's denizens constantly test their masters for any flicker of weakness.

The roots of orcish demonology trace back to Draenor, where the demon lord Kil'jaeden seduced Gul'dan with the promise of supreme power. Gul'dan founded the secretive Shadow Council and transformed many shaman—starting with members of the Blackrock clan—into masters of fel magic. The rampant use of demonic magic withered Draenor's fertile plains into barren red wasteland, heralding the Old Horde's invasion through the Dark Portal. In human lands, the Kirin Tor forbade demonology and hunted down illicit summonings, yet ambitious mages regularly succumbed to the lure of untamed sorcery.

In the modern era, warlocks walk a razor's edge between utility and execution. In Stormwind, practitioners meet hidden away in gloomy tavern basements, far from the watchful eyes of the Cathedral of Light. In Orgrimmar, they cluster in the shadowed chasms of the Cleft of Shadows, kept under scrutiny by Thrall's shamanistic regime. Warriors are the quintessential frontline combatants of Azeroth, mastering heavy plate armor, shields, and nearly every form of martial weaponry. Fueling their most devastating strikes with pure combat rage, they charge into the thick of battle to defend weaker allies or carve through enemy ranks. They are found across every race and civilization, serving as everything from stalwart city guards and royal champions to wandering mercenaries.

Warriors rely neither on divine prayers nor arcane incantations. Their power stems entirely from physical endurance, battlefield discipline, and an exhaustive mastery of weaponry. Clad in the heaviest plate mail, they dictate the frontline. Some fight behind towering shields to withstand punishing assaults and draw peril away from spellcasters and archers. Others step forward with two-handed polearms, axes, and greatswords, or wade into melee wielding a blade in each hand to cleave through whole formations.

In the furnace of battle, pain and blood ignite a warrior's inner fire. Known simply as rage, this resource swells as warriors inflict and absorb punishment. Rather than yielding to exhaustion or bleeding wounds, seasoned fighters channel this combat fury directly into bone-shattering strikes, sweeping whirlwinds of steel, and deafening battle cries that bolster nearby comrades while shattering enemy morale.

Unlike classes tied to specific creeds or elemental patrons, the warrior tradition is universal to every race on Azeroth. Stormwind relies on the disciplined knight-champions of the Brotherhood of the Horse, Ironforge marshals its stout Forgeguard, and the Horde rallies around orcish blademasters, tauren braves, and Forsaken Deathguards. Westfall was once the breadbasket of the Kingdom of Stormwind, but Stormwind withdrew its troops and left the people defenseless. In the vacuum, the masked bandits of the Defias Brotherhood swept across the plains, seizing family homesteads, commandeering iron mines, and extorting local farmers. Based at Sentinel Tower atop Sentinel Hill, the Militia maintains a tenuous perimeter across the region's main thoroughfares. Before the War of the Three Hammers, the Wildhammers lived in the foothills around Ironforge. When High King Modimus Anvilmar died, civil war fractured the dwarven kingdom, and the victorious Bronzebeards claimed Ironforge for themselves. Thane Khardros led his clan north to establish a magnificent hold inside the peak of Grim Batol. Yet peace was short-lived: the defeated Dark Irons soon laid siege to the fortress. While Khardros personally slew the Dark Iron sorceress Modgud, her dying curse blighted the mountain so deeply that the halls became uninhabitable. Refusing an invitation to move back under Bronzebeard rule, the Wildhammers chose self-reliance, marching north into the forests and rocky crags of the Hinterlands.

In the lush highlands of their new realm, the Wildhammers built Aerie Peak. Forging enchanted stormhammers in secluded aviaries, the Wildhammers became the finest aerial cavalry in Azeroth. Even as the human kingdoms squabbled and fractured in later years, the Wildhammers remained steadfast partners of King Terenas Menethil II. Worgen are fierce, lupine humanoids cursed with uncontrollable primal rage, moving upright yet hunting with bestial swiftness. Once thought to be mere nightmares conjured from other planes, these savage pack-hunters now terrorize Silverpine Forest, Ashenvale, and Duskwood.

Long before their recent emergence in Lordaeron and Kalimdor, wolf-men were whispered of in folktales and cautionary fables. In reality, their origins date back over nine millennia to the War of the Satyr. Seeking to harness the untamed fury of the wolf Ancient Goldrinn, radical night elf druids led by Ralaar Fangfire embraced the forbidden wolf pack form. When combined with the sacred Scythe of Elune, the magic violently backfired, transforming them into ferocious lupine monsters driven by bloodlust. Incapable of distinguishing friend from foe, their virulent bite spread the affliction to fellow night elves. To halt the nightmare, Malfurion Stormrage and the Cenarion Circle banished the cursed shapeshifters beneath the sacred boughs of Daral'nir into an eternal slumber within the Emerald Dream.

During the Third War, as the Scourge hordes overran Lordaeron and descended toward the Greymane Wall, Archmage Arugal sought a weapon to save Gilneas. Drawing from the forbidden research of the Dalaran wizard Ur, Arugal pierced the veil and summoned the slumbering beasts into Silverpine Forest. The summoned worgen devastated the undead invaders with savage abandon, but the archmage could not leash their fury. The beasts turned on Gilnean soldiers, spreading their curse through fang and claw. Driven mad by guilt and fascination, Arugal adopted the monsters as his children, seizing Baron Silverlaine's ancestral seat—now rechristened Shadowfang Keep—and cursing nearby villagers into monstrous nocturnal servitude.

Across the sea in Kalimdor, another summoning unleashed the worgen anew. Channelling the ancient relic, she called forth wolf-men to tear apart the demonic satyrs. Yet as battles raged, Velinde realized that the scythe had slipped beyond her command—the beasts began to manifest without her consent, slipping into the dark forests of Ashenvale and beyond. Now roaming in wild, feral packs, the worgen spread terror wherever the shadow of their moonlit hunts falls.
